fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Mask Behind Legal Personhood", "body": "Chance introduces the artificial person as a body created by law and legally distinct from the human behind it, then traces person to the Latin persona, which he reads as a stage mask tied to sound. He calls the courtroom a kind of spell play of spoken words. Beth argues that a corporate straw man is manufactured at birth, that nobody is taught the difference, and that repeating the corporate version of your name back to an official places you inside their jurisdiction. Chance links this to the many personas people wear to fit the collective."}, {"title": "Corporation, Franchise and the Sovereign Self", "body": "Chance reads the 1828 Webster's definition of a corporation as a body authorized to act as a single person, then zooms in on franchise, which he says means to incorporate, so that being enfranchised makes a person a subcorporation. Beth notes that calling someone disenfranchised is an inversion. He adds that corporation shares a root with body, so the only corporation worth belonging to is your own, and he treats the corporation sole, one person acting as one, as a clue: unify the parts of yourself and become your own king."}, {"title": "Archetypes as Allies or Shadows", "body": "Beth explains that an archetype held in conscious awareness becomes a tool and an ally, while one buried in the unconscious uses the person, leaving them two dimensional and lost in mysteria, the term both of them keep borrowing. She says anything in shadow fights for attention so a person can become more aware. Chance adds that shadow archetypes animate self hate and a distorted view of the body, and Beth traces that self hate, and hatred of others, to one root program, the fear of not surviving."}, {"title": "The Child, Betrayal and the Hero's Journey", "body": "Beth describes the shadow child as dissociating under fear, terrified of betrayal and abandonment, and calls the legal system a massive betrayal that people dread although it has already happened. Chance adds, from her book, that the hero's journey only begins once the betrayal is faced, since innocence matures into knowing. Beth says innocence becomes a superpower in legal encounters, citing Tom Barnett, who answers demands with a playful 'Are you sure?', and describes moving from resenting the study of law to looking forward to it."}, {"title": "Victimhood, Perpetrators and the Collective", "body": "Beth calls the victim archetype a bid for fake energy, with a disclaimer that people who were truly harmed should not be told to stop being victims, and says healing requires taking responsibility. Using an emotional scale she credits to David Hawkins and Lester Levinson, she says rising from fear into anger can turn the victim into a perpetrator, and she claims the system and police welcome that anger. Chance observes that victimhood has become a cultural currency and warns that if everyone sacrifices for the collective, everyone is sacrificed."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Beth Martens returns to bring us a psychological analysis of law, from a spiritual and archetypal perspective. What is a persona, and how does it pertain to our corporate existence? What are the foundational character archetypes of the perpetrators of legal fictions, and how does our own archetypal posture help or hinder our successes in and against the system?

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Selling Out: The Prostitute Archetype in Law", "body": "Chance opens the second hour on the prostitute archetype, picturing a corporate clown in a work uniform and suggesting that misused creativity runs through the law world, driven by safety, wealth and power. Beth says anyone moving through the legal system will eventually be offered a deal that tempts them against their values, and she holds up a man she interviewed with Alphonse, who refused every concession, as the light side of the pattern. Complying to stay safe, she argues, leaves a person evacuated and easier to steer, since each compromise makes the next one cheaper."}, {"title": "The Saboteur and the Fear of Success", "body": "Chance describes the saboteur as self blindfolded, blaming luck rather than owning responsibility, and later reads it as an inverted Uranus: freedom from responsibility instead of freedom through it. Beth says success frightens the saboteur more than failure, because it demands energy and responsibility, and the hardest stretch comes just before a breakthrough. She says people sabotage themselves in court by handing over jurisdiction, and that those insisting nobody has free will remain stuck in mysteria. Her counsel is to hold your position, because you always have the choice."}, {"title": "The King in Shadow and in Light", "body": "Beth says the shadow king's drug is power, an addiction that never satisfies, which she believes explains why those in control keep tightening it, and she calls the court itself a king in its shadow. She warns that sovereign, as she understands the word, means ruler with dominion over others, so it may be the wrong goal. The awakened king, in her telling, answers to God, serves the people and raises other kings. Chance adds that the shadow king fears looking weak, while both of them favor asking questions over issuing orders."}, {"title": "The Alchemist and the Inner Mirror", "body": "Beth names the alchemist as the archetype that follows the king, bringing deep healing and a way of working with energy rather than force, and she recommends inner work before anyone enters a legal fight so they stay steady instead of handing power over. Chance recalls first sensing the alchemist in himself when tending groups caught in the same loop, finding the stuck feeling and resolving it within himself. Beth agrees the problem is felt inside even when it appears outside, and adds that the shadow alchemist weaponizes symbolic language to deceive."}, {"title": "Words as Symbols and the I Am", "body": "Beth argues that legal writing leans on dog Latin, where words work as symbols that illustrate rather than describe, so a name in capitals points somewhere other than the living person. Chance agrees that language should only describe, and applies the point to identity: you can feel sadness without being sad. Beth calls mistaken identity the one problem beneath every other and points to the I Am. Chance offers a theory that hypnosis plants borrowed mysteria, and closes with his view that the judge imitates God."}]
